plain_english: The next step is to make sure we don't work for worthless things or work in vain. This means two things: don't chase what you can't get, and don't discover too late — after all your hard work — that what you wanted was foolish. In other words, make sure your efforts actually lead somewhere, and that the results are worth the effort you put in. Most sadness comes from one of two places: either you fail to get what you want, or you succeed and then feel ashamed of what you were chasing.
original_excerpt: The next point to these will be to take care that we do not labour for what is vain, or labour in vain: that is to say, neither to desire what we are not able to obtain, nor yet, having obtained our desire too late, and after much toil to discover the folly of our wishes: in other words, that our labour may not be without result, and that the result may not be unworthy of our labour: for as a rule sadness arises from one of these two things, either from want of success or from being ashamed of having succeeded.

plain_english: We need to stop all this endless running around that most people do. They wander from house to house, from theaters to markets. They stick their noses into everyone else's business and always look like they have something important to do. Ask one of them as he leaves his house, "Where are you going?" He'll say, "I honestly don't know, but I'll meet some people and do something." They drift around looking for something to do. But they don't do what they planned — they do whatever happens to come up. They move around without any purpose or plan, like ants crawling over bushes. The ants climb to the top, then back down to the bottom, and get nowhere. Many people live their whole lives this way. You could call it restless laziness.
original_excerpt: We must limit the running to and fro which most men practise, rambling about houses, theatres, and market-places. They mind other men's business, and always seem as though they themselves had something to do. If you ask one of them as he comes out of his own door, "Whither are you going?" he will answer, "By Hercules, I do not know: but I shall see some people and do something." They wander purposelessly seeking for something to do, and do, not what they have made up their minds to do, but what has casually fallen in their way. They move uselessly and without any plan, just like ants crawling over bushes, which creep up to the top and then down to the bottom again without gaining anything. Many men spend their lives in exactly the same fashion, which one may call a state of restless indolence.

plain_english: You would feel sorry for some people when you see them rushing around like their house is on fire. They bump into everyone they meet and drag themselves and others along with them. But where are they going? To greet someone who won't even greet them back. To attend a funeral for someone they didn't know. To hear the verdict for someone who's always in court. To watch the wedding of someone who gets married all the time. They'll follow some important person's chair around, and sometimes even help carry it. Then they come home exhausted from doing nothing useful. They swear they don't even know why they went out or where they've been. And the next day? They'll do the exact same pointless routine all over again.
original_excerpt: You would pity some of them when you see them running as if their house was on fire: they actually jostle all whom they meet, and hurry along themselves and others with them, though all the while they are going to salute some one who will not return their greeting, or to attend the funeral of some one whom they did not know: they are going to hear the verdict on one who often goes to law, or to see the wedding of one who often gets married: they will follow a man's litter, and in some places will even carry it: afterwards returning home weary with idleness, they swear that they themselves do not know why they went out, or where they have been, and on the following day they will wander through the same round again.

plain_english: Make sure all your work has a purpose. Keep some goal in mind. Restless people aren't driven by hard work — they're driven crazy by wrong ideas. Even they don't move around without hope. They get excited by how things look on the surface. Their confused minds can't see that it's all pointless. It's the same with everyone who goes out to join the crowds in the streets. They wander around the city for worthless, empty reasons. Dawn drives them out even when they have nothing to do. They push their way to many doors, greet one doorkeeper after another, get turned away from many houses — and discover that the hardest person to find at home is themselves. This bad habit leads to the worst vice of all: gossiping and prying into public and private secrets. They learn many things that are dangerous both to tell and to hear.
original_excerpt: Let all your work, therefore, have some purpose, and keep some object in view: these restless people are not made restless by labour, but are driven out of their minds by mistaken ideas: for even they do not put themselves in motion without any hope: they are excited by the outward appearance of something, and their crazy mind cannot see its futility. In the same way every one of those who walk out to swell the crowd in the streets, is led round the city by worthless and empty reasons; the dawn drives him forth, although he has nothing to do, and after he has pushed his way into many men's doors, and saluted their nomenclators one after the other, and been turned away from many others, he finds that the most difficult person of all to find at home is himself. From this evil habit comes that worst of all vices, talebearing and prying into public and private secrets, and the knowledge of many things which it is neither safe to tell nor safe to listen to.
